# Performance claims

This report is the single document that owns the project's performance claims and their provenance.
It is generated from `spec/bench/claims.tsv`, the record `bench/claims/run.sh` writes, and the prose
below; the marked block is the only copy of the numbers, so a hand-edited number fails
`TestGeneratedPerformanceClaimsIsCurrent` and `TestPerformanceClaimsMatchMeasurement` instead of
drifting away from the record. Every earlier figure, and the reason it moved, is recorded in the
provenance section of this same document.

<!-- performance-claims -->
Measured on Linux x86_64, 16 logical CPUs. Load: 1-minute load average 1.66 before the run; precondition below 4.00 (0.25 per logical CPU on 16 logical CPUs). Toolchain: clang version 22.1.8 (Fedora 22.1.8-4.fc44); go version go1.26.9-X:nodwarf5 linux/amd64; rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28) (Fedora 1.99.0-1.fc44); Erlang/OTP 26. Flags: qkc default -O3 -flto=thin; C clang -O3 -flto=thin; Rust rustc -O; Go go build (default); Erlang erlc (default). Skipped controls: none.

What is counted: in-process wall time: clock()/clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)/Instant::now()/time.Now()/timer:tc(); process startup and printing excluded; every row prints its result as a checksum. Evidence: every workload prints its result as the checksum; the harness fails when the checksum changes between runs; the C, Rust and Go fib controls read the argument from argv so the optimizer cannot constant-fold the recursion.

## What each workload measures

- **fib** — recursive `fib(n)`, one call per timed run. The QuarkLang and Erlang sources carry the
  argument; the C, Rust and Go controls read it from argv (C through a `volatile`) so the optimizer
  cannot fold the recursion at compile time. Every run prints the result, which is the checksum.
- **sum** — one `sum(ident, 0, 1e9)` call in QuarkLang, which the interpreter and compiler resolve to
  the arithmetic-series closed form, against a plain Go loop over the same terms. The elapsed time is
  measured in process; the QuarkLang row is below `clock()`'s one-microsecond resolution on this
  build, and the record says so instead of inventing a finer number.
- **fib(20) latency** — the P50 and P99 thresholds of 1000 `fib(20)` calls. A threshold is found by
  counting how many calls finish at or below it and binary-searching that count, so the histogram
  itself is not in the timed loop. The row's value is the threshold in microseconds, not the total
  runtime.
- **interpreter versus native** — the same six checked-in programs run once by `quark` and once as a
  `qkc` binary, with the timed region inside the program on both sides. Output parity is required:
  the harness fails when the two checksums differ.

Two measured results contradict the table this report replaced, and they stay visible rather than
being tuned away: the Erlang `fib(30)` control is far faster than the withdrawn four-digit figure, and
the `str` row's native binary is slower than the interpreter on this build, so the earlier
"quadratic on both paths" note did not survive. The block reports the medians and the spread for both
rows; no workload was reshaped to restore the earlier ordering.

## Method

`bench/claims/run.sh` builds every program once, runs it once untimed, then runs it five times and
reports the median, minimum, maximum, standard deviation and `(max-min)/median` spread. No run is
presented as "the best". `--record` writes `spec/bench/claims.tsv` and refuses to do so unless the
host's 1-minute load average is below 0.25 per logical CPU, using the same probe as the tide harness;
the measured load is part of the record and is stated above.

The record's authority depends on its shape, so the harness has no `--n` override: every workload's
round count and the five-run count are fixed in the checked-in sources and in
`spec/bench/claims-shapes.tsv`. `--record` refuses any other shape, and the generator rejects a
record whose rows do not match that table. `--record --dry-run` validates the shape without measuring
or writing, and `--quick` takes one run per row for CI smoke and can never be recorded.

A missing Rust or Erlang toolchain is skipped explicitly and named under `skipped` in the record; no
number is invented for it. The record is generated once on the reference class named in the block and
checked in; CI runs the quick harness to keep the workloads working, and the drift gate compares the
generated text rather than rerunning the timing on a different machine.

## Reproducing and checking

```sh
./bench/claims/run.sh                    # print the record (5 timed runs per row)
./bench/claims/run.sh --record           # on a quiet host: write spec/bench/claims.tsv and regenerate this report
./bench/claims/run.sh --record --dry-run # validate the canonical shape, print the plan, write nothing
./bench/claims/run.sh --quick            # one run per row: CI smoke
./bench/claims/run.sh --compile-only     # build the C controls with -Werror, measure nothing
go generate ./internal/benchgen          # render this report and docs/tide-benchmark.md
go run ./cmd/qkbench -check -suite claims
```

After `--record`, run `go generate ./internal/benchgen`; this report is the only document that carries
the block. `TestGeneratedPerformanceClaimsIsCurrent` runs the check in the ordinary `go test ./...`
gate, and `TestPerformanceClaimsMatchMeasurement` compares this report with the record, so a quoted
number cannot survive a record change on its own. No other document embeds a second copy: README and
`spec/STANDARD.md` link here instead.

## What the numbers say

On the reference class the QuarkLang `fib` rows are slower than the C control, and the latency rows are
slower at both percentiles; both paths use LLVM `-O3`, so the gap is in the code the compiler emits,
not in the choice of backend. The earlier "same as C" wording did not survive measurement and was
corrected, not footnoted. The interpreter is not a speed feature; it exists to remove the compile step
and keep REPL state. There is no checked-in CPython control, so no comparison with CPython is quoted.
The block reports the medians, ranges and spread for every row; no workload was reshaped to restore an
earlier ordering. `scripts/bench-report.sh` remains a manual report: it writes no record, so its output
is not quoted.

## Provenance: every earlier performance claim

This section inventories every performance claim that used to live in `README.md`, the documentation
under `docs/`, and the standard, and states for each one where it came from and whether any checked-in
harness produces it. It records the input to the rule that a performance number must be generated from
a record, not typed by hand.

Status legend:

- **generated** — a checked-in harness writes a record, the generator renders the block, and a test
  fails when a quoted copy and the record disagree.
- **harness, no record** — a script can produce a similar measurement, but it writes nothing, applies
  no load gate, records no spread or checksum, and no test compares it with prose.
- **manual** — the number exists only where it is quoted; nothing in the repository can reproduce it.
- **historical** — a one-off observation of a revision that no longer exists; kept as history, not as a
  claim about the current build.

The tide family already satisfied the rule before this consolidation: `bench/tide/run.sh` writes
`spec/bench/tide.tsv` behind a load gate and a canonical-shape guard, `internal/benchgen` renders
[`tide-benchmark.md`](tide-benchmark.md), and `TestTideClaimsMatchMeasurement` compares that single
document with the record.

Locations name the revision the inventory was taken from; the README's line numbers moved when the
manual tables were removed, and the generated blocks have since moved into their single documents.
This inventory records both the original state and the disposition that was applied. The `Status`
column is the final state: **generated** claims are produced by `bench/claims/run.sh` from
`spec/bench/claims.tsv` and checked by `TestGeneratedPerformanceClaimsIsCurrent` and
`TestPerformanceClaimsMatchMeasurement` against the block above; **corrected** claims
survive only as a qualitative pointer to the generated block; **withdrawn** claims had no checked-in
producer and their numbers were removed from the live text; **historical** figures stay only in notes
that carry a banner saying they are not claims about the current build; **excluded** rows are
correctness or status facts, not performance claims.

## Why this matters

Three of the README claims were wrong or unsupportable as written:

1. R-02/R-09/R-10 mix different source programs. `bench/qk/fib.qk` computes `fib(30)`, while the C,
   Rust, Go and Erlang sources compute `fib(35)`, and `bench/Makefile` compiles `examples/fib.qk` for
   the QuarkLang target. The quoted "fib(35) 21 ms (C: 22 ms)" therefore does not correspond to any
   one checked-in command.
2. R-12 labels two values per language as "P99" without saying what the pair is, and no source exists.
   It cannot be reproduced as stated.
3. R-17's "Before" column refers to binaries that are not in the tree; the numbers are history, not a
   statement about the current build.

## Disposition

The rule is one sentence: a number a reader can act on must come from a record, and every other number
must stop looking like one.

- **Automate** (checked-in workload, comparison controls where the claim compares, load gate, canonical
  shape, record, generated block, drift/claim test): the cross-language fib family (R-02, R-05, R-09,
  R-10), the closed-form `sum` (R-06, R-13), the latency claim (R-03, R-12), and the interpreter versus
  native table (R-15, R-16). The same harness and generator as the tide block are extended, not
  duplicated.
- **Withdraw or mark historical** (no checked-in producer, and the measurement cannot be repeated on
  this tree): R-07, R-08, R-11, R-17 through R-25, D-03 through D-10, and the retrospective parts of
  D-01/D-02. Numbers that a reader could mistake for a current measurement are removed from the live
  text or explicitly labelled as a historical observation of an earlier revision.
- **Keep generated**: R-14, D-11, S-01.
- **Leave excluded**: S-03 and D-12 through D-14, which are correctness/status facts, not performance
  claims.

The standard's revision log records the earlier figures and why they moved, including any claim that
had to be withdrawn because it could not be put under the machinery.

## Corrections from the measurement

The claims harness replaced the manual figures with one record taken on the reference class

table and its spreads are in the generated block above; these are the moves that matter.

The "measured" column is a snapshot for provenance; the generated block above is the authority. The
measured rows are not adjusted to preserve an earlier narrative. Where the record contradicts the
prose, the prose was corrected or the claim was withdrawn; the standard's revision log 0.8.15 records
the same moves.

A claim that can be measured again belongs in the record above. A claim that cannot is recorded
above with the reason it moved, and it does not keep a number where a reader could take it as a fact
about the current build.
